https://www.local10.com/news/local/2026/.text: MIAMI — Influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate appeared before a federal magistrate in Miami on Monday for the first time since they were arrested to face rape and sex trafficking charges in the United Kingdom. The Tates have been held in federal detention following their arrest on Saturday. In the coming weeks, a U.S. district judge will consider whether they meet the conditions for extradition. An attorney for the brothers, Joseph McBride, has blasted the charges as “filth and slander,” as well as “salacious and defamatory.” Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in southeastern England. The allegations, spanning 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. Their lawyer said in a statement Saturday that he believed the arrests were “greenlighted by a low-level functionary” at the Justice Department without input from leadership. But the Justice Department told The Associated Press that the arrests were approved by leadership of its Criminal Division. McBride, outside of the Miami federal courthouse, said he plans to fight extradition on the Tates’ behalf. “We are going to fight them at every turn, and at every corner, because they are American citizens,” McBride said. McBride claims the new allegations are politically-motivated. “I’ve never seen evidence that indicates these guys are guilty of anything,” he said. “They are being punished and attacked for what they say and not for what they have done. You can love them, you can hate them, but nobody should go to jail for free speech.” Taking a swipe at the U.K., McBride said, “We will make sure that we exhaust all remedies before they are sent over to the communist regime previously known as the free place of the United Kingdom.” McBride, explaining his ties representing people in Jan. 6 cases, implied that he believes President Donald Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio would be sympathetic to the case. “I believe that Marco Rubio and the rest of the trump administration are not fans of communism, for prosecuting people for free speech, this is one of the reasons why they were elected,” he said, noting that after the Jan. 6 prosecutions, “I would just think as a matter of principle, based on the reasons why they were elected, that they would not want to see two free citizens go to a country where they are going to be thrown in jail for political reasons.” According to the U.S. Department of Justice, “If the court finds the fugitive to be extraditable, it certifies the extradition and sends the record to the Secretary of State, who decides whether to surrender the fugitive.” Former federal prosecutor David Weinstein said even though the charges the Tates face are not considered “political offenses” by definition, under the extradition treaty, “the executive branch of the U.S., including the president, can block the extradition request if they determine that the request was politically motivated.” “So yes, President Trump is able to help prevent an extradition to the U.K. if he wanted to,” Weinstein said. The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the U.S., Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. Their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny has made them among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities. The dual U.S. and British citizens moved to Romania in 2016. They were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. Last year, they were allowed to leave Romania and flew to Florida.

Home Paid news feed Foto Agerpres Press Monitoring Bucharest Phone: +4 021.2076.110 Pasca challenges CoE Human Rights Commissioner over alleged use of unverified information in Dumbrava case Category: English Date: 2026-07-22 17:29:46 Foto: Grigore POPESCU / AGERPRES Photo Viorel Pasca, founder of the care facilities in Dumbrava, Bihor County - currently under DIICOT investigation - has published an open letter addressed to the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, in which he challenges the statements made in the Commissioner's letter to the Romanian Prime Minister regarding the Dumbrava case and argues that the European official relied on unverified information. In the open letter posted on Facebook, Pasca writes that he read with interest Michael O'Flaherty's message to Romania's Prime Minister and appreciates the Commissioner's concern for vulnerable persons; however, he criticises the references made to the activities carried out at the Dumbrava locations, maintaining that the Council of Europe official should have verified the information before including it in the letter. 'I don't know where you received your information from, but I believe that, regardless of the source, you should first have verified whether it is true and whether those who provided it are credible sources and have evidence to support it. Do not forget that the presumption of innocence should also apply in Romania,' Pasca wrote. Responding to the letter's mention of 'illegal homes', Pasca rejects the characterisation, noting: 'I can tell you that Dumbrava has never operated as a centre or care home. All locations were, in fact, residential houses in which Romanian citizens lived and had their domicile. None of them lived there illegally, none were detained, abused or tortured as has been alleged in mass media. Those who wished to leave did so whenever they wanted, and they returned of their own free will whenever they wished.' Pasca further disapproves of the manner in which, in his view, information about the activities in Dumbrava was collected and disseminated, asserting that some publicly cited sources presented false information. He also expresses disagreement with the Commissioner's assessment of the intervention carried out by the Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) in the Dumbrava case. 'If you consider such an intervention to be 'normal', necessary and justified - legally, logistically, morally or from any other point of view - then I am firmly convinced that what you have been told has no connection with reality, and that you have 'fallen into the trap' of those who supplied you with this information,' he wrote. In conclusion, Pasca asks the Commissioner for Human Rights to carefully verify information before making public statements and argues that, in his view, it would have been appropriate to await the court's decision in the Dumbrava case. The letter is signed, 'With highest consideration, Viorel Pasca'. The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, published on Tuesday a letter addressed to Romanian Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan, following his visit to Romania between May 26 - 29 this year, in which he formulates a series of recommendations concerning the long-term care system for older persons, the Strasbourg-based organisation said. The Commissioner welcomes progress in the reform of social services and the dedication of staff working in care centres for older persons. At the same time, he expresses concern regarding several challenges, including the insufficient recognition of residents as full rights-holders, the shortage of services, and the difficulties faced by vulnerable persons in accessing care. He also draws attention to care centres operating without licences and calls for a thorough and independent investigation into the Dumbrava case. According to the letter dated July 10, the matter concerns the unlicensed care centre in the village of Dumbrava, Bihor County, which is alleged to have housed thousands of vulnerable persons in abusive conditions and where more than one thousand deaths were reportedly recorded. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images South Korea Starbucks Korea raided by police after ‘Tank Day’ campaign sparks public outrage Coffee chain has faced backlash over marketing promotion tied to anniversary of Gwangju massacre Associated Press in Seoul Thu 6 Aug 2026 03.45 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 03.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google South Korean police have raided the headquarters of Starbucks Korea as part of an investigation into a marketing campaign accused of trivialising the country’s 1980s pro-democracy movement. Investigators searched the building in southern Seoul on Tuesday, police said on Wednesday. No further details were released, although South Korean media reported that officers also searched the homes of the Starbucks Korea executives. How a Starbucks marketing stunt spiralled into mass boycotts in South Korea Read more The coffee chain triggered a public outcry after launching a range of stainless-steel reusable tumblers it called “SS Tank” and declaring 18 May “Tank Day”. The date marks the anniversary of the 1980 Gwangju uprising, when pro-democracy demonstrators were brutally suppressed by South Korea’s then military-backed government. The campaign also used the slogan “Thwack it on the table!”, which many interpreted as a reference to a notorious 1987 police claim that the student activist Park Jong-chul died after investigators “hit the desk with a thwack”. Authorities had falsely used the phrase to conceal the fact that Park had died by torture during an interrogation. The backlash over the coffee chain’s marketing campaign prompted Shinsegae Group, which owns a 67.5% stake in Starbucks Korea, to cancel the promotion within hours and dismiss the company’s chief executive . The Shinsegae chair, Chung Yong-jin, later issued a televised apology. Starbucks Korea closed all of its stores nationwide on 22 June for mandatory training in history and social awareness. The police investigation was launched after complaints from relatives of victims of the Gwangju crackdown, in which, official records say, about 200 people were killed. South Korea’s transition to democracy gained momentum in 1987, when the authoritarian president Chun Doo-hwan, whose government had overseen the Gwangju crackdown, accepted constitutional reforms introducing direct presidential elections after months of nationwide pro-democracy protests. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/19/russ.text: Russians fearing a new military mobilisation are leaving the country in advance of possible restrictions on departure, according to the anti-war project Ark, after requests for emergency assistance and emigration advice from Russia have nearly octupled since the start of the summer.The surge coincides with Russia's State Duma elections, which began on Friday and run through Sunday.Kremlin critics and several Western governments have accused Moscow of planning to announce a new call-up to beef up its troops in its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine after the vote concludes, allowing an unpopular measure to avoid affecting the election.Russia's Vladimir Putin has dismissed mobilisation rumours as "utter nonsense," but independent Russian media have counted 17 official denials of an imminent draft since the summer.Jan Slovitsky, a human rights activist and coordinator of the Ark project, said the current wave was driven by lessons learned from 2022."Since mid-July a wave of panic has been rising in Russia, linked to the risk of mobilisation, fuel shortages and lack of internet access," he told Ark's network from Yerevan, where he is assisting new arrivals."People are leaving in advance because they have seen what happened during previous waves. And Armenia is facing a migration crisis, if we are not already in the thick of it."'How to leave' online search spikesThe number of daily requests for relocation assistance has risen from around 70 to 120 since July, according to organisations helping Russians move abroad.Yandex and Google searches for "how to leave" and "mobilisation" reached their highest level since early 2023 during the summer and the first ten days of September, according to independent Russian media analysis.Preparations for a possible call-up are already visible. Tens of thousands of people have received mobilisation notices setting out the steps required if called up, and an electronic register of summonses has been introduced under which an exit ban takes effect automatically when a notice is issued.In early September, passport control officers in Krasnodar detained a 24-year-old resident of Rostov region who had completed his military service in 2024 and served him with a notice banning him from leaving the country, the first such case reported at that crossing.Daniil Neonov, a former candidate for municipal deputy in the Moscow City Duma, described leaving at the last moment."If I had waited another day or two, they would most likely not have let me leave, because they would have blocked my exit," he said. "I received an electronic summons. But I still managed to get out."Fear of mobilisation has also spread to members of the elite and draft office staff, according to international media reports claiming officials have begun opening foreign bank accounts and moving assets abroad.In August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned of the risk of mobilisation in Russia, citing intelligence data.Kyiv described a Kremlin plan to rapidly call up several hundred thousand Russians by the end of the year, with at least as many again the following year. Moscow has not commented on those claims.Neighbouring countries firstArrivals are heading primarily to visa-free destinations: Armenia, Georgia and Kazakhstan. Yerevan said in recent days it was ready to assist Russians arriving in the country.The exact scale of the current wave is unknown, but it is likely less intense than the exodus of 2022, when between 600,000 and 700,000 people left Russia within weeks of the partial mobilisation announcement, according to independent estimates.That mobilisation has never been formally cancelled, and those called up then have not been demobilised."It is very sad to leave Russia," said a 28-year-old marketing specialist, whose name was withheld for security reasons."My family lives here, my elderly grandparents live here. My girlfriend is here too, she is still in her medical residency, and it is very hard for me to leave her behind."Russia's Duma elections, running from 18 to 20 September, include only parties that back Moscow's war in Ukraine. Yabloko, whose platform called for an immediate ceasefire and peace talks, was barred from standing by the Supreme Court in August.

https://outsidethebeltway.com/german-far.text: German Far-Right Dominates State Election European leaders are grappling with the implications for rising populism and nativism across the continent. Comments The Guardian (“ Europe facing ‘grave moment’ as far-right AfD wins German poll and pledges to work with Elon Musk “): Mainstream politicians around Europe have expressed alarm after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept to a historic state election victory in Germany, while nationalist figures cheered the result as a mandate for change. While falling just short of an absolute majority, the AfD surged into first place in the Saxony-Anhalt state election on Sunday, exit polls ⁠showed, putting the far right within reach ​of power at ‌the state level for ‌the first time since the second world war. “It ‌clearly sends out a very, very worrying signal,” France’s finance minister, Roland Lescure, said on Monday. “This shows that we face a major challenge in the face of ‌a populist wave which is spreading around the world today and which we must ​resist.” Lescure’s comments echoed similar remarks on Sunday evening by France’s European affairs minister, Benjamin Haddad, who posted on social media: “To see the far-right ⁠prevail in the German regional election marks a very ​grave ​moment for Europe.” Haddad added: “We must listen ​with humility ‌to the ​anger, ​fears and worries and duly respond to these concerns. But nationalism and xenophobia will never be the answer. We cannot forget our history.” ‌Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, said on Monday the AfD’s win was “a very worrying sign”. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, said on Sunday night in Poland, “only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany”. Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, described the election result as “terrible news … because it concerns a political force that is antithetical to liberal and western values”. The reaction was not limited to Europe. Elon Musk congratulated the far-right party on its election victory with a “Well done!” on his social media platform X, prompting Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, to thank the nativist US tech billionaire for his support. “If we take on responsibility here, I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation,” Siegmund wrote. “Germany would then once again be a place worth investing in. Best regards from Saxony-Anhalt!” The US president, Donald Trump, whose White House has made no secret of its support for Europe’s nationalist far-right parties, posted a screenshot of the projected election result on his Truth Social platform without any comment. Kirill Dmitriev, Russia’s presidential envoy, took a screen grab of Trump’s post and praised a “historic win for the pragmatic AfD”. The AfD is pro-Kremlin, has called for an end to aid for Ukraine and and refugee status for Ukrainians. The former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán, who was heavily defeated in elections earlier this year, celebrated AfD’s win, describing it as “a huge night for Germany and Europe” and adding: “Buckle up. This is just the beginning!” It’s a strange world, indeed, where Italy’s own far-right government is expressing alarm while the US President is siding with Russian and Hungarian autocrats. Mark Landler, NYT (“ Far-Right Victory in German State Sends a Signal to Europe “): When a far-right party won a landslide victory on Sunday in a small state in eastern Germany, its reverberations could be felt from Downing Street in London to the Élysée Palace in Paris. Rarely has the result of a regional election been viewed with such portent for the fate of democracy in Europe. This wasn’t just any European country; it was Germany, a country that has relentlessly isolated far-right political parties since the calamity of Nazism. And it wasn’t just a strange outlier, but rather the latest step in a steady, decade-long march that has brought the far right ever closer to the fulcrum of power in Europe. With elections scheduled across Europe next year, the striking success of the party, Alternative for Germany, could be a harbinger of further far-right victories, according to analysts, as well as a template for how they can be engineered. Its populist, anti-immigrant message echoes those of nationalist leaders in Britain, France, Italy and Spain, all countries where voters harbor many of the same grievances as those in Germany. French voters will elect a new president next spring. An election is due in Spain by August, and in Italy by the end of next year. Far-right candidates are surging in all of them, threatening incumbents blamed for systemic problems with their countries’ economies. “Developed Europe is going through a version of sophisticated state failure,” said Mujtaba Rahman, an analyst who specializes in Europe at Eurasia Group, a political risk consultancy. “Governments are unable to address cost-of-living concerns. They are not able to deliver for their voters.” In Germany, rising prices and high unemployment helped win the far-right party, known by its German initials, AfD, more than twice the number of votes as Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s center-right incumbent party. The result laid bare a divide between Europeans who see the far right as a threat to democracy, and a growing number who see it as democracy’s savior. The former warn that the far right will dismantle checks and balances, while treating minorities as second-class citizens. The latter see it as a bulwark against an out-of-touch elite that has eroded their national identity and endangered their livelihoods. We’ve seen this trend since at least 2016, when Brits voted to leave the EU and Americans elected Donald Trump. Working class voters across the West are angry about, well, everything. On issues ranging from immigration to globalization to social issues, they feel that mainstream parties have not served them well. Still, this is a local race, not one to govern Germany. Further, it’s a state that was part of the former East Germany for decades, so less steeped in the backlash against Nazism than their western countrymen. And, as noted when I previewed this a few days ago, unlike America’s first-past-the-post method, the German electoral system does not necessarily give the plurality winner control. Because the AfD appeared to fall just short of an outright majority, according to near-final results, it may not end up governing Saxony-Anhalt, the state where the election was held. Rival parties have vowed that they would not form a coalition government with the AfD, whose leaders have used Nazi slogans and minimized the Holocaust. The AfD is designated as a “suspected” extremist group by German intelligence, partly because the group portrays Germans of immigrant backgrounds as second-class citizens. Al Jazeera produced this chart from the official results: That AfD fell just shy of a majority, winning 39 of the 42 seats needed to form a government outright, is astounding. That it dwarfed the combined total (26.5%) of the two traditional parties—indeed, the delta between that total and theirs is exactly CDU’s vote—even more so. Indeed, it requires combining the five parties that finished behind AfD to surpass them. If none of the other parties is willing to join a government with AfD—and they all claim that to be the case–it’s going to take one oddball coalition to form an alternative. Which, given the election outcome, may well backfire. AfD voters will rightly be angry to be shut out. Regardless, who runs Saxony-Anhalt is far less interesting than what it may portend for the continent. Still, the result could hobble Mr. Merz if members of his party blame him for the loss, at a time when Germany’s leadership in Europe was already faltering. Mr. Merz’s standing has deteriorated so badly that political analysts talk openly of his ouster, a once-far-fetched scenario in German politics. “It’s a big concern in Europe,” said Mr. Rahman, who previously worked for the European Union’s civil service. “A weak Germany, with a chancellor who is coming unstuck and being forced to deal with domestic problems, is bad and will ultimately subtract from Europe’s ability to confront its challenges.” Worries among centrists about France, where President Emmanuel Macron will step down next spring, are no less acute. Marine Le Pen, the candidate of France’s main far-right party, the National Rally, holds a commanding lead in first-round polls, and has even finished first in recent second-round matchups. That puts her closer to power than at any time in her 14 years of seeking the presidency. A far-right government in Paris, Mr. Rahman said, would destabilize the European Union in a way that no other national election has, given France’s size, nuclear arsenal and founding role in the European project. It might also bring an end to the so-called cordon sanitaire, under which mainstream parties in France, as in Germany, have refused to enter governing coalitions with the far right. “In both countries, the antifascist front that had prevailed since the end of the Second World War seems on the verge of collapse,” said Philippe Marlière, a professor of French and European politics at University College London. In Spain, analysts said the far-right Vox Party could elbow its way into the next coalition government, with the current Socialist-led government tarnished by corruption scandals and an immigration crisis. In Britain, the governing Labour Party ousted its unpopular prime minister, Keir Starmer, in July to try to regain traction against a fast-rising far-right party, Reform U.K. Landler does sound an optimistic note: Still, the rise of the far right is not inexorable. Reform’s success has been rudely interrupted by a series of financial scandals involving its firebrand leader, Nigel Farage. That has given the Labour government, under a new prime minister, Andy Burnham, some unexpected breathing room. In April, the far-right leader of Hungary, Prime Minister Viktor Orban, was swept out of power after 16 years, a casualty of widespread perceptions that his government was corrupt, inattentive to the economy, and had picked needless battles with the European Union. The defeat of his Fidesz party gave hope to mainstream politicians that the far right, too, is vulnerable. Alternatively, it may be that the problem is incumbency. Unlike the others, Orban wasn’t an outsider railing against the unjust policies of those in power; he had to actually govern and be judged on the results. Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, whose populist party has neofascist roots, offers a playbook to other like-minded leaders. Having modulated her tone on issues like Ukraine and the European Union, she recently celebrated her government’s becoming the longest continuously serving in the history of the Italian Republic.
